micros.title: Warm-up: Four Operations on Rationals
micros.description: Revise adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing rational numbers in fraction form, including negatives.
outcomes: Can compute a±b, a×b, a÷b for any two rationals
Can handle signs correctly through each operation

micros.title: Closure, Commutativity and Associativity
micros.description: Test which of the four operations keep rationals closed, commutative and associative — and catch subtraction and division failing the last two.
outcomes: Can state which properties hold for which operations
Can produce a counterexample when a property fails

question.prompt: Which of these is TRUE for rational numbers?

options.text: a − b = b − a for all rationals a, b
a ÷ b = b ÷ a whenever both sides are defined
a × b = b × a for all rationals a, b
(a − b) − c = a − (b − c) for all rationals
options.diagnosis: Assumed associativity extends to subtraction; try a=5, b=3, c=1: 1 ≠ 3.

question.explanation: Only addition and multiplication are commutative and associative for rationals. Check 3 − 5 = −2 but 5 − 3 = 2, and 1 ÷ 2 ≠ 2 ÷ 1. One counterexample kills a property.

micros.title: Identities, Opposites and Reciprocals
micros.description: Fix 0 and 1 as the additive and multiplicative identities, and sharply separate the additive inverse (opposite) from the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) — noting 0 has no reciprocal.
outcomes: Can give the additive and multiplicative inverse of any rational
Can explain why 0 has no reciprocal

question.prompt: What is the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of −5/8?

options.diagnosis: Flipped the fraction but also flipped the sign — a reciprocal keeps the sign, since the product must be +1.

question.explanation: The reciprocal r must satisfy (−5/8) × r = 1, so r = −8/5. The OPPOSITE of −5/8 is 5/8 (sums to 0) — that is the additive inverse, a different job. And 0 never works: nothing times 0 gives 1.

micros.title: Distributivity and Smart Computation
micros.description: Use a(b + c) = ab + ac to reorganise messy rational calculations into easy ones.
outcomes: Can apply distributivity to simplify computations like 3/7 × 5/6 + 3/7 × 1/6

micros.title: Rationals on the Number Line
micros.description: Locate any rational, positive or negative, on the number line by subdividing unit intervals.
outcomes: Can mark rationals like −7/4 on a number line accurately

micros.title: Density: Rationals Between Rationals
micros.description: Discover that between ANY two rationals lie infinitely many more, using averages and common denominators.
outcomes: Can find n rationals between two given rationals
Can argue why the process never runs out

question.prompt: How many rational numbers lie between 1/4 and 1/2?

options.text: Only those with denominator 4: none in this case
options.diagnosis: Restricted attention to one denominator; rewriting as 2/8 and 4/8, then 4/16 and 8/16, keeps exposing new rationals.

question.explanation: The average of two distinct rationals is a new rational strictly between them, and you can average again forever: 1/4 < 3/8 < 1/2, then 1/4 < 5/16 < 3/8, ... Rationals are dense.

micros.title: Perfect Squares and Their Fingerprints
micros.description: Generate squares 1–30 and read off their properties: possible unit digits, behaviour of trailing zeros, and sums of odd numbers.
outcomes: Can list unit digits a perfect square can end in
Can reject candidates like 4058 as perfect squares by inspection

question.prompt: Exactly one of these numbers is a perfect square. Which one COULD it be, judging by unit digits?

options.diagnosis: Ends in 7 — no square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8, so it is ruled out immediately.

question.explanation: A perfect square can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. Endings 3, 8 and 7 disqualify the other three instantly; 5776 ends in 6 and is in fact 76². The unit-digit test rejects, it never confirms — but here it leaves only one candidate.

micros.title: Squaring Fractions and Decimals
micros.description: Square rationals like 3/4 and 0.4, tracking why squaring a number between 0 and 1 makes it SMALLER and where the decimal point lands.
outcomes: Can square any fraction or decimal correctly
Can explain why (0.4)² < 0.4

question.prompt: Compute: (0.4)²

options.diagnosis: Squared 4 but dropped the decimal point entirely.

question.explanation: (0.4)² = 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16 — two decimal places in, two + two = ... count decimal places: 1 + 1 = 2 places, giving 0.16. Squaring is NOT doubling (that would be 0.8), and 4² = 16 must keep its decimal shift.

micros.title: Square Roots by Prime Factorisation
micros.description: Find square roots of perfect squares by pairing prime factors, and find the smallest multiplier/divisor that makes a number a perfect square.
outcomes: Can compute √ of a perfect square via factor pairs
Can find the least number to multiply by to reach a perfect square

micros.title: Square Roots by Long Division
micros.description: Use the long-division algorithm for square roots of large perfect squares and decimals.
outcomes: Can extract √ of 4-5 digit numbers by long division
Can extend the method past the decimal point

micros.title: Estimating Square Roots
micros.description: Trap non-perfect squares between consecutive perfect squares to estimate roots like √60 ≈ 7.7.
outcomes: Can state between which two integers √n lies
Can give a one-decimal estimate of a square root

micros.title: √ Does Not Split Over + and −
micros.description: Confront the error √(a+b) = √a + √b with numeric ambushes like √(9+16), and establish that roots split only over × and ÷.
outcomes: Can evaluate √(a+b) correctly by adding first
Can state for which operations √ distributes

question.prompt: Evaluate: √(9 + 16)

options.diagnosis: Halved 25 — treated square-rooting as halving.
Added correctly but forgot to take the root at all.

question.explanation: Add first: 9 + 16 = 25, and √25 = 5. Splitting gives √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7 — a different, wrong number. The root distributes over × (√(9×16) = 3×4 = 12 ✓) but never over + or −.

micros.title: Cubes and Their Patterns
micros.description: Build cubes 1–20 as n × n × n (not n × 3), and explore unit-digit patterns — cubes, unlike squares, can end in ANY digit.
outcomes: Can compute cubes of numbers up to 20
Can state the unit digit of a cube from the unit digit of the number

question.prompt: Compute: 4³

options.diagnosis: Squared instead of cubed — stopped one multiplication early.
Computed 3⁴ (or a wrong table fact) — swapped base and exponent.

question.explanation: 4³ means 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. The exponent counts how many copies of 4 are multiplied — it is never a multiplier itself (that would be 4 × 3 = 12).

micros.title: Cubes of Negative Numbers
micros.description: Establish that an odd number of negative factors leaves the product negative: cubing preserves sign.
outcomes: Can cube negative integers and rationals correctly
Can explain the sign via counting negative factors

question.prompt: Compute: (−5)³

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 3 AND applied the even-power sign rule — two errors stacked.

question.explanation: (−5)³ = (−5)(−5)(−5): the first pair gives +25, the third factor flips it to −125. THREE negative signs — an odd count — always leave a negative product. Even powers kill the sign; odd powers keep it.

micros.title: Cube Roots by Prime Factorisation
micros.description: Find cube roots by grouping prime factors in TRIPLES, and find the smallest multiplier that turns a number into a perfect cube.
outcomes: Can compute ∛ of a perfect cube via factor triples
Can find the least factor needed to complete a perfect cube

question.prompt: Find: ∛216

options.diagnosis: Took the square root instead of the cube root.

question.explanation: 216 = 2×2×2 × 3×3×3 = (2×3)³, so ∛216 = 6. Check: 6×6×6 = 216. Dividing by 3 (216 ÷ 3 = 72) or halving are answers to different questions — a root undoes REPEATED MULTIPLICATION, not multiplication by 3.

micros.title: Estimating Cube Roots of Perfect Cubes
micros.description: Use the unit digit and thousands-grouping trick to read off cube roots of perfect cubes up to six digits.
outcomes: Can find ∛ of a 4-6 digit perfect cube by the two-group estimation method

micros.title: Warm-up: Ratios and Percentage Change
micros.description: Revise converting between fractions, ratios and per cents, and computing increase/decrease as a percentage of the ORIGINAL value.
outcomes: Can find x% of a quantity and a percentage change
Can identify the base quantity a per cent acts on

micros.title: Discount and Marked Price
micros.description: Work the trio marked price, discount, sale price — the discount per cent always bites the MARKED price.
outcomes: Can compute sale price from MP and discount %
Can recover MP or discount % from the other two

question.prompt: A jacket is marked ₹800 and sold at a 15% discount. What is the sale price?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted ₹15 — treated the per cent as a rupee amount.
Computed the discount amount but reported it as the sale price — stopped a step early.

question.explanation: Discount = 15% of the MARKED price = 0.15 × 800 = ₹120, so sale price = 800 − 120 = ₹680. (₹692 comes from discounting some other base, e.g. taking 15% off ₹800 minus tax or applying 13.5%: the discount must act on ₹800 itself.)

micros.title: Successive Percentage Changes
micros.description: Chain two percentage changes multiplicatively and see why 10% off then 20% off is 28% off — never 30% — and why +10% then −10% does not restore the price.
outcomes: Can compute the net effect of two successive % changes
Can explain why successive per cents don't add

question.prompt: A shop gives successive discounts of 10% and then 20% on a ₹1000 item. What is the final price?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by the discount fractions instead of the REMAINING fractions (0.90 and 0.80).
Applied 10% then 20% but computed the second discount on ₹1000 again instead of on ₹900.

question.explanation: After 10% off: 1000 × 0.90 = ₹900. After 20% off THAT: 900 × 0.80 = ₹720. Net effect 28% off, not 30% — the second discount acts on an already-reduced price, so successive per cents multiply (0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72), never add.

micros.title: Sales Tax, VAT and GST
micros.description: Add tax percentages onto bills and extract the pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive total.
outcomes: Can compute a bill including tax
Can find the original price given a tax-inclusive amount

micros.title: Compound Interest: Interest on Interest
micros.description: Contrast CI with SI year by year on the same principal, then compress the growth into A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.
outcomes: Can compute CI for 2-3 years both stepwise and by formula
Can say exactly where CI and SI diverge and why

question.prompt: ₹1000 is invested at 10% per annum, compounded annually. How much interest has it earned after 2 years?

options.diagnosis: Computed only one year's interest.
Reported the final AMOUNT instead of the interest earned.

question.explanation: Year 1: 10% of 1000 = ₹100, balance ₹1100. Year 2: 10% of 1100 = ₹110 — interest now earns interest. Total ₹210. Simple interest would pay 10% of the ORIGINAL ₹1000 both years: ₹200. The ₹10 gap is exactly the interest on year 1's interest.

micros.title: CI Applications: Growth and Depreciation
micros.description: Apply the compound formula to population growth, bacterial growth and depreciation (negative rate), including half-yearly compounding.
outcomes: Can adapt A = P(1 ± r/100)ⁿ to growth and depreciation contexts
Can halve the rate and double the periods for half-yearly compounding

micros.title: Warm-up: Laws of Exponents
micros.description: Revise aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ with positive exponents — exponents ADD and SUBTRACT, they are never multiplied or divided across the laws.
outcomes: Can apply the product and quotient laws with positive integer exponents

question.prompt: Simplify: a⁸ ÷ a²

options.diagnosis: Added the exponents — used the product law on a quotient.
Divided the bases as well as handling the exponents — the base a stays.

question.explanation: a⁸ ÷ a² cancels two of the eight factors of a, leaving a⁶: exponents SUBTRACT (8 − 2 = 6). Dividing them (8 ÷ 2 = 4) answers a different question — write out the factors once and the cancellation is visible.

micros.title: What a Negative Exponent Means
micros.description: Extend the descending pattern 2³, 2², 2¹, 2⁰, ... to force 2⁻ⁿ = 1/2ⁿ: a negative exponent flips into a reciprocal, it never makes the value negative.
outcomes: Can evaluate powers with negative exponents
Can explain 2⁻³ = 1/8 via the halving pattern

question.prompt: Evaluate: 2⁻³

options.diagnosis: Flipped to the reciprocal AND attached a minus sign — the flip alone does the whole job.

question.explanation: Follow the pattern: 2³=8, 2²=4, 2¹=2, 2⁰=1, and each step divides by 2 — so 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4, 2⁻³ = 1/8. The minus sign in the exponent means 'reciprocal', not 'negative': 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8, a positive number.

micros.title: Exponent Laws with Negative Exponents
micros.description: Run all the laws — product, quotient, power of a power, power of a product — with integer (including negative) exponents.
outcomes: Can simplify expressions like (2⁻³ × 2⁷) ÷ 2² fully
Can combine laws in multi-step simplifications

micros.title: Standard Form for Large Numbers
micros.description: Write large numbers like 149,600,000 km as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10, counting decimal SHIFTS rather than zeros.
outcomes: Can convert large numbers to standard form and back
Can compare two numbers written in standard form

micros.title: Standard Form for Small Numbers
micros.description: Use negative powers of 10 for very small measurements (0.00052 m = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴ m), pinning down the sign and size of the exponent by counting shifts.
outcomes: Can convert small decimals to standard form with the right negative exponent

question.prompt: Write 0.00052 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: The power is consistent, but standard form needs the leading factor between 1 and 10 — 52 is too big.

question.explanation: Move the decimal point until one nonzero digit leads: 0.00052 → 5.2 needs 4 shifts right, so the exponent is −4 (small number ⇒ negative power). Counting the three zeros gives −3, one off: count SHIFTS of the point, not zeros. Check: 5.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.2 ÷ 10000 = 0.00052.

micros.title: Direct or Inverse? Recognising the Relationship
micros.description: Sort real situations by asking 'when one doubles, does the other double or halve?' — and spot relationships that are NEITHER.
outcomes: Can classify a situation as direct, inverse, or neither
Can justify the classification with a doubling test

question.prompt: Which situation shows INVERSE proportion?

options.text: More pipes filling a tank, less time to fill it
More metres of cloth, higher total cost
options.diagnosis: That is DIRECT proportion — both grow together.

options.text: A child's age and their height
More workers on a job, more days to finish

question.explanation: Inverse proportion: doubling one quantity HALVES the other, keeping the product constant — twice the pipes, half the time. Cloth/cost is direct (constant ratio). Age/height grows together but with no fixed ratio — proportional thinking doesn't apply at all there.

micros.title: Solving Direct Proportion Problems
micros.description: Set up x/y = constant (or the unitary method) for direct variation — a multiplicative relationship, not 'add the same amount'.
outcomes: Can solve for the missing value in a direct proportion
Can verify the answer keeps the ratio constant

question.prompt: A car uses 6 litres of petrol for 90 km. How far can it travel on 10 litres?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 90 by 6/10 instead of 10/6 — inverted the scale factor.
Multiplied 90 × 10 without dividing by 6 — skipped the unitary step.

question.explanation: Distance per litre is constant: 90 ÷ 6 = 15 km/L, so 10 L gives 150 km. The relationship is multiplicative (×10/6), not additive — '4 more litres so 4 more km' (94) treats it as y = x + k.

micros.title: Solving Inverse Proportion Problems
micros.description: Use x₁y₁ = x₂y₂ — the PRODUCT stays constant — for inverse variation, resisting both the additive shortcut and the direct-proportion reflex.
outcomes: Can solve for the missing value in an inverse proportion
Can check the answer by comparing products

question.prompt: 6 workers can build a wall in 12 days. Working at the same rate, how long would 8 workers take?

options.diagnosis: Adjusted additively in the wrong direction — added the 2 extra workers to the days.

question.explanation: Total work = 6 × 12 = 72 worker-days; with 8 workers, 72 ÷ 8 = 9 days. The PRODUCT stays fixed, so more workers ⇒ proportionally fewer days. Scaling up (16) applies direct proportion; '2 more workers, 2 fewer days' (10) pretends the trade-off is additive.

micros.title: Mixed and Multi-step Proportion Problems
micros.description: Tackle problems mixing both variation types (speed-time-distance, recipes scaled for more people in less time), choosing the model before computing.
outcomes: Can solve two-step problems involving both direct and inverse variation

micros.title: Numbers in General Form
micros.description: Write any two- or three-digit numeral algebraically — 'ab' means 10a + b, never a × b — and use it to explain simple number tricks.
outcomes: Can expand a numeral into general form and back
Can express 'reverse the digits' algebraically

question.prompt: A two-digit number has tens digit a and units digit b. Which expression equals the number?

options.diagnosis: Summed the digits — that loses the place value entirely (72 would equal 9).
Right structure, wrong places — this is the REVERSED number.

question.explanation: The tens digit counts tens: 7 tens and 2 units is 10×7 + 2 = 72. Writing digits side by side is positional notation, not multiplication — a×b for 72 would give 14.

micros.title: Adding and Subtracting Reversed Numbers
micros.description: Prove with general form why (10a+b) + (10b+a) is always divisible by 11, and the difference by 9 — the classic reversal results.
outcomes: Can prove the 11 and 9 divisibility facts for reversed two-digit numbers
Can extend the argument to three-digit reversals (divisibility by 99)

micros.title: Letters for Digits: Cryptarithm Puzzles
micros.description: Solve addition and multiplication puzzles where letters stand for digits, respecting the rules: one digit per letter, 0-9 only, carries tracked, no leading zeros.
outcomes: Can solve one- and two-carry cryptarithms systematically
Can state and use the digit constraints explicitly

question.prompt: In the puzzle A1 + 1B = B0 (each letter one digit, B0 a two-digit number), what is A?

options.diagnosis: Ignored the carry from the units column: 1 + B ends in 0 forces B = 9 WITH a carry into the tens.
Made the sum's tens work without carrying, but then A1 has a leading-zero problem and the units column fails.

question.explanation: Units: 1 + B ends in 0, so B = 9, carry 1. Tens: A + 1 + 1(carry) = B = 9, so A = 7. Check: 71 + 19 = 90. ✓ Every letter must stay a single digit 0-9 and every carry must be honoured.

micros.title: Why the Divisibility Tests Work
micros.description: Use general form to justify the tests for 2, 5, 10 (last digit) and 3, 9 (digit sum) — and see why 3's test looks at ALL digits, and why divisible-by-3 does not mean divisible-by-9.
outcomes: Can apply the tests for 2, 3, 5, 9, 10 correctly
Can explain via 10 = 9 + 1 why digit sums govern 3 and 9

question.prompt: Which of these numbers is divisible by 9?

options.diagnosis: Ends in 8, an even digit — but evenness tests 2, not 9; digit sum 28 is not a multiple of 9.

question.explanation: Test with digit sums: 3+4+3+8 = 18, a multiple of 9, so 3438 works (3438 = 9 × 382). 1279 contains a 9 but its digit sum is 19 — a 9 'anywhere' proves nothing. 1236 has digit sum 12: divisible by 3, NOT by 9 — the 3-test passing never guarantees the 9-test.

micros.title: Warm-up: Transposing with Inverse Operations
micros.description: Revise solving ax + b = c by moving terms with their operations INVERTED — plus becomes minus, times becomes divide.
outcomes: Can solve one-side linear equations fluently
Can name the inverse operation used at each step

micros.title: Variables on Both Sides
micros.description: Collect variable terms on one side and constants on the other, changing the SIGN of every term that crosses the equals sign.
outcomes: Can solve equations like 2x + 5 = x + 9
Can verify a solution by substitution

question.prompt: Solve: 2x + 5 = x + 9

options.diagnosis: Reached 2x = 4 by also moving the x with its sign unchanged, then divided — check by substituting: 9 ≠ 11.

question.explanation: Move x left and 5 right, flipping signs: 2x − x = 9 − 5, so x = 4. Check: 2(4)+5 = 13 = 4+9. ✓ Every term that crosses '=' swaps sign; x = 14 keeps +5 alive as +5, and x = 4/3 comes from 2x + x = 4.

micros.title: Equations with Brackets
micros.description: Expand brackets — multiplying EVERY term inside — before collecting, as in 3(x − 2) = 2(x + 1) + 1.
outcomes: Can solve equations with bracketed terms on either side

micros.title: Clearing Fractions
micros.description: Multiply BOTH SIDES — every single term — by the LCM of the denominators to turn fractional equations into integer ones.
outcomes: Can clear denominators correctly and solve
Can spot the error of multiplying only the fraction term

question.prompt: Solve: x/2 + 3 = 5

options.diagnosis: Computed (5 − 3) ÷ 2 — divided by 2 at the end instead of multiplying.
Multiplied through by 2 twice — once clearing, once again at the end.

question.explanation: Multiply EVERY term by 2: x + 6 = 10, so x = 4. Check: 4/2 + 3 = 5. ✓ Multiplying only the x/2 term gives x + 3 = 10 ⇒ x = 7 — but then the two sides were scaled unequally, breaking the equation.

micros.title: Equations Reducible to Linear Form
micros.description: Solve equations like (x + 1)/(2x + 3) = 3/8 by cross-multiplication, checking the solution keeps denominators nonzero.
outcomes: Can cross-multiply and solve rational equations that reduce to linear
Can reject values that zero a denominator

micros.title: Word Problems: Set Up, Solve, ANSWER
micros.description: Translate age, number, perimeter and money stories into equations — then finish: solve fully and answer the question actually asked.
outcomes: Can model a word problem as a linear equation
Can present the final answer in the problem's terms, checked against the story

question.prompt: Sum of two numbers is 95. One exceeds the other by 15. The problem asks for the SMALLER number. You reach x + (x + 15) = 95. What is the answer?

options.diagnosis: Restated a given from the problem instead of solving.

question.explanation: 2x + 15 = 95 ⇒ 2x = 80 ⇒ x = 40, and x was DEFINED as the smaller number. 55 is the larger one — a correct solve answering the wrong question. And '2x = 80' is a checkpoint, not an answer: always finish, then reread what was asked.

micros.title: Multiplying Monomials
micros.description: Multiply coefficients and ADD exponents of like bases: 3x × 4x = 12x², handling several variables at once.
outcomes: Can multiply two or three monomials correctly
Can track coefficients and exponents separately

question.prompt: Multiply: 3x × 4x

options.diagnosis: Added the coefficients AND lost the x·x — treated × as + throughout.

question.explanation: 3x × 4x = (3 × 4)(x × x) = 12x². Coefficients MULTIPLY (3×4=12) and x·x = x² — dropping either piece gives 12x or 7x².

micros.title: Multiplying Binomials: Every Term Meets Every Term
micros.description: Expand (x + 2)(x + 3) by distributing each term of the first bracket over ALL of the second — four products, then collect.
outcomes: Can expand a binomial × binomial fully
Can verify an expansion numerically with a test value

question.prompt: Expand: (x + 2)(x + 3)

options.diagnosis: Added 2 + 3 for the constant term instead of multiplying.
Used the product 2×3 for BOTH the middle and last terms.

question.explanation: Four products: x·x + x·3 + 2·x + 2·3 = x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6. Pairing only firsts and lasts (x² + 6) skips the two cross terms. Check with x = 1: (3)(4) = 12 = 1 + 5 + 6. ✓

micros.title: The Identity (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
micros.description: Derive the square-of-a-sum identity by multiplication and by area picture — the middle term 2ab is the two rectangles a term-by-term squaring forgets.
outcomes: Can expand (a + b)² for numeric and algebraic a, b
Can point to 2ab in the area model

question.prompt: Expand: (x + 5)²

options.diagnosis: Included only ONE of the two cross rectangles — the middle term is 2·x·5, not x·5.
Doubled 5 for the last term too — only the middle term carries the factor 2; the last is 5².

question.explanation: (x+5)² = (x+5)(x+5) = x² + 5x + 5x + 25 = x² + 10x + 25. Test x = 1: (6)² = 36 = 1 + 10 + 25 ✓, while x² + 25 gives 26 ✗ — squaring term by term drops the two 5x rectangles.

micros.title: The Identity (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
micros.description: Adapt the sum identity to differences, nailing the signs: middle term negative, last term still POSITIVE.
outcomes: Can expand (a − b)² with correct signs
Can explain why b² keeps a plus sign

question.prompt: Expand: (x − 4)²

options.diagnosis: Expanded (x + 4)² — the sign of the middle term must follow the sign inside the bracket.

question.explanation: (x−4)(x−4) = x² − 4x − 4x + 16 = x² − 8x + 16. The last term is (−4)(−4) = +16 — negative × negative. Check x = 5: (1)² = 1 = 25 − 40 + 16 ✓; x² − 16 gives 9 ✗.

micros.title: The Identity (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²
micros.description: See the cross terms cancel in (a + b)(a − b), leaving a difference of squares — and distinguish it firmly from (a − b)².
outcomes: Can expand (a + b)(a − b) instantly
Can say which of a² − b² and (a − b)² goes with which expression

micros.title: Identities as Mental-Math Weapons
micros.description: Compute 103², 98², 51 × 49 and similar in the head by choosing the right identity around a round number.
outcomes: Can pick and apply the right identity for a numeric shortcut
Can compute products like 51 × 49 mentally

question.prompt: Use an identity to compute 51 × 49 mentally.

options.diagnosis: Computed 50² but forgot to subtract the b² = 1 that the identity requires.
Computed 49² — squared one factor instead of using (50+1)(50−1).
Added instead of subtracting: a² − b² needs 2500 − 1, not 2500 + 9 or any sum.

question.explanation: 51 × 49 = (50 + 1)(50 − 1) = 50² − 1² = 2500 − 1 = 2499. The cross terms ±50 cancel — that cancellation is the whole trick.

micros.title: Taking Out Common Factors
micros.description: Factor the HCF out of every term — 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3) — and check by expanding back.
outcomes: Can factor out the greatest common monomial factor
Can verify a factorisation by re-expanding

question.prompt: Factorise: 6x + 9

options.diagnosis: Divided 9 by... something else — 9 ÷ 3 = 3; expand to check: 3(2x+6) = 6x + 18 ✗.
6 is not a factor of 9 — the common factor of 6 and 9 is 3.

question.explanation: HCF of 6x and 9 is 3: 6x + 9 = 3·2x + 3·3 = 3(2x + 3). EVERY term must be divided by the factor taken out — expanding 3(2x + 9) = 6x + 27 exposes the un-divided 9.

micros.title: Factorisation by Regrouping
micros.description: Group four-term expressions like ax + bx + ay + by into pairs sharing a factor, then pull out the common bracket.
outcomes: Can factor four-term expressions by grouping
Can re-group when the first pairing fails

micros.title: Factoring with the Identities
micros.description: Run the three identities backwards: spot a² + 2ab + b², a² − 2ab + b², and especially a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b) — which is NOT (a − b)².
outcomes: Can recognise and factor perfect-square trinomials
Can factor any difference of squares

question.prompt: Factorise: x² − 16

options.diagnosis: Expanding gives x² − 6x − 16 — the middle term must vanish, so the two numbers must be opposites.
That expands to x² − 16x — you factored out x from a term that has none.

question.explanation: x² − 16 = x² − 4² = (x + 4)(x − 4): the +4x and −4x cross terms cancel. (x − 4)² = x² − 8x + 16 is a different beast — a difference OF squares is not the square OF a difference. Check x = 5: 25 − 16 = 9 = 9 × 1. ✓

micros.title: Factorising x² + bx + c by Splitting the Middle Term
micros.description: Hunt for two numbers whose SUM is the middle coefficient b and whose PRODUCT is the constant c, then split and group.
outcomes: Can factor monic quadratics by splitting the middle term
Can state which target is the sum and which the product

question.prompt: Factorise: x² + 5x + 6

options.diagnosis: Right numbers, wrong signs — expanding gives x² − 5x + 6.
6 and −1 have product −6 and sum 5 — the product must be +6 AND the sum +5 simultaneously.

question.explanation: Need two numbers with sum 5 (the x-coefficient) and product 6 (the constant): 2 and 3. So x² + 5x + 6 = (x+2)(x+3). Swapping the roles — sum 6, product 5 — yields 1 and 5, which fails the expansion check: (x+1)(x+5) = x² + 6x + 5.

micros.title: Dividing Algebraic Expressions
micros.description: Divide polynomials by monomials by factoring first — the divisor must cancel from EVERY term, or from a common FACTOR, never from a single term of a sum.
outcomes: Can divide a polynomial by a monomial via factorisation
Can spot and refute illegal single-term cancellation

question.prompt: Simplify: (5x + 10) ÷ 5

options.diagnosis: Divided 10 by 2 instead of 5 — arithmetic slip in the second term.

question.explanation: Factor first: 5x + 10 = 5(x + 2), so dividing by 5 leaves x + 2. Cancelling the 5 against only ONE term (giving x + 10 or 5x + 2) breaks the value — test x = 1: (15) ÷ 5 = 3 = 1 + 2 ✓, but 1 + 10 = 11 ✗.

micros.title: The Coordinate Plane: Plotting Points
micros.description: Set up x- and y-axes and plot ordered pairs, establishing that ORDER matters: (3, 5) and (5, 3) are different points.
outcomes: Can plot and read off points in the first quadrant
Can explain why coordinate order matters

question.prompt: Which statement about the points (3, 5) and (5, 3) is correct?

options.text: They are the same point only if the axes use the same scale
options.diagnosis: Scale changes where a point is DRAWN, never which point it is — coordinates are scale-independent addresses.

options.text: (3, 5) lies on the x-axis and (5, 3) on the y-axis
options.diagnosis: Neither has a zero coordinate, so neither lies on an axis.

question.explanation: An ordered pair reads (x, y): (3, 5) is 3 across and 5 up; (5, 3) is 5 across and 3 up — different addresses. Order is the whole point of ORDERED pairs.

micros.title: Points on the Axes and the Origin
micros.description: Pin down where (0, y) and (x, 0) live: a zero x-coordinate means NO horizontal movement — the point sits on the y-axis.
outcomes: Can place points with a zero coordinate correctly
Can characterise the axes as 'y = 0' and 'x = 0' point sets

question.prompt: Where does the point (0, 4) lie?

options.diagnosis: Only (0, 0) is the origin — one zero coordinate is not enough.
That would be (4, 4); the first coordinate here is 0, so there is no horizontal move.

question.explanation: (0, 4) says: move 0 across, then 4 up — you never leave the vertical axis. The '0 goes with x' pairing tempts you toward the x-axis, but a zero x-coordinate KEEPS you on the y-axis.

micros.title: Reading Line Graphs and Scales
micros.description: Extract information from time-series line graphs, always reading axis labels, units and scales before comparing anything.
outcomes: Can read values and trends off a line graph
Can explain how a changed scale changes apparent steepness

micros.title: Drawing Graphs of Linear Relationships
micros.description: Tabulate values for relationships like y = 2x + 1 or simple-interest-vs-time, plot, and draw the line through them.
outcomes: Can build a table and draw a straight-line graph
Can use the graph to read off unplotted values

micros.title: Every Point on the Line Counts
micros.description: Establish that a linear graph is a continuum: any point on the line — plotted or not — satisfies the relationship, and coordinates can be read at ANY x.
outcomes: Can decide whether a given point lies on a drawn line
Can interpolate values between tabled points

question.prompt: You plotted y = 2x for x = 1, 2, 3 and joined the points with a line. Is (2.5, 5) on the graph?

options.text: Yes — every point of the line satisfies y = 2x, and 5 = 2 × 2.5
No — only the three plotted points belong to the graph
No — x = 2.5 is not a whole number, so it is not allowed
Yes, but only because it is halfway between two plotted points
options.diagnosis: Midpoint luck is not the reason — (2.5, 5) qualifies because it SATISFIES the equation; so does (2.7, 5.4).

question.explanation: The line IS the set of all (x, y) with y = 2x — infinitely many points. The table just gave three anchors to draw it. Since 2 × 2.5 = 5, the point (2.5, 5) lies on the graph, along with every other satisfying pair.

micros.title: Polygons: Convex, Concave, Regular
micros.description: Classify polygons by number of sides, convexity, and regularity, revising the vocabulary of diagonals and interior angles.
outcomes: Can classify a polygon as convex/concave and regular/irregular
Can count the diagonals of small polygons

micros.title: Interior Angle Sums of Polygons
micros.description: Triangulate an n-gon into (n − 2) triangles to get the angle-sum formula — 360° belongs to quadrilaterals ONLY.
outcomes: Can compute the interior angle sum of any polygon
Can find one interior angle of a regular n-gon

question.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon?

options.diagnosis: Used 100° per triangle or an arithmetic slip — each of the 3 triangles contributes 180°.
Used n − 1 = 4 triangles — a pentagon triangulates into n − 2 = 3.

question.explanation: From one vertex a pentagon splits into 3 triangles: (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°. The 360° figure is the QUADRILATERAL's sum (2 triangles) — every extra side adds another 180°.

micros.title: Exterior Angles Always Total 360°
micros.description: Walk around any convex polygon to see the exterior angles complete one full turn — a constant 360° regardless of n.
outcomes: Can use the exterior-angle sum to find unknown angles
Can find the number of sides of a regular polygon from one exterior angle

micros.title: Parallelogram Properties: Sides and Angles
micros.description: Derive from parallel sides that opposite sides and opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY.
outcomes: Can find all angles of a parallelogram from one
Can justify each property via parallel lines and transversals

question.prompt: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 70°. What is ∠B (adjacent to A)?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted from 360° — the whole quadrilateral's sum, not the co-interior pair's 180°.
Made the pair complementary (90°) instead of supplementary (180°).

question.explanation: AD ∥ BC with AB as transversal makes ∠A and ∠B co-interior: ∠B = 180° − 70° = 110°. EQUAL is the privilege of OPPOSITE angles (∠C = 70°); neighbours must add to 180°.

micros.title: Diagonals of a Parallelogram
micros.description: Show the diagonals BISECT each other — but are equal only in rectangles, and perpendicular only in rhombuses.
outcomes: Can use diagonal bisection to find lengths
Can state which special quadrilaterals have equal or perpendicular diagonals

question.prompt: Which property do the diagonals of EVERY parallelogram have?

options.diagnosis: That is the rhombus's special property — a generic parallelogram's diagonals cross at other angles.
Again special to the rhombus (and square) — draw a long thin parallelogram to see it fail.

question.explanation: In any parallelogram the diagonals cut each other exactly in half. EQUAL diagonals are the rectangle's upgrade; a slanted parallelogram visibly has one long and one short diagonal.

micros.title: The Quadrilateral Family Tree
micros.description: Order trapezium, kite, parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square by inclusion: every square IS a rhombus IS a parallelogram — the arrows never reverse.
outcomes: Can decide the truth of 'every X is a Y' claims for special quadrilaterals
Can draw the inclusion diagram from memory

question.prompt: Which statement is TRUE?

options.diagnosis: Rectangles ARE parallelograms — the special cases sit INSIDE the general class, not beside it.

question.explanation: A rhombus needs four equal sides; a square has them (plus right angles), so every square is a rhombus. Going the other way fails: a 2×5 rectangle is no square, a tilted rhombus is no square. Definitions include — extra properties narrow, never exclude.

micros.title: Why Five Measurements?
micros.description: Discover with cut-out strips that four given sides leave a quadrilateral FLOPPY — unlike a triangle — and that five well-chosen parts pin it down.
outcomes: Can demonstrate that four sides do not fix a quadrilateral
Can list the five standard measurement combinations that do

question.prompt: You are given all four side lengths of a quadrilateral, and nothing else. Can you construct it uniquely?

options.text: No — the shape can still flex; a fifth measurement is needed
Yes — four sides fix a quadrilateral just as three sides fix a triangle
Yes, provided the four sides are all different
options.diagnosis: Distinct side lengths don't stop the flexing — the angles are still free.

options.text: No — you would need all eight measurements (4 sides + 4 angles)

question.explanation: A four-sided frame with hinged corners flexes into infinitely many quadrilaterals (push a square into ever-flatter rhombuses). A diagonal braces it — that is the fifth measurement. Triangles alone are rigid; and five SUITABLE parts suffice, you never need all eight.

micros.title: Constructing with Four Sides and a Diagonal
micros.description: Split the target into two triangles along the given diagonal, build each with compass arcs, and check feasibility with the triangle inequality first.
outcomes: Can construct a quadrilateral from 4 sides + 1 diagonal
Can reject infeasible data before drawing

question.prompt: You must construct quadrilateral PQRS with PQ = 4 cm, QR = 3 cm and diagonal PR = 8 cm (plus two more sides). What do you notice BEFORE drawing?

options.text: Triangle PQR is impossible: 4 + 3 < 8 violates the triangle inequality
Nothing — start drawing and adjust the vertices until it looks right
Nothing is wrong; any five measurements give a constructible quadrilateral
PR must equal PQ + QR exactly, so change PR to 7 cm
options.diagnosis: Equality gives a DEGENERATE (flat) triangle — the inequality must be strict, but any PR < 7 works, not only 7.

question.explanation: The diagonal PR closes triangle PQR, so its sides must satisfy PQ + QR > PR. Here 4 + 3 = 7 < 8: the arcs will never intersect. Feasibility is checked in each half-triangle BEFORE touching the compass — construction is deduction, not adjustment.

micros.title: Constructing with Two Diagonals and Three Sides
micros.description: Locate vertices as intersections of compass arcs when both diagonals and three sides are given.
outcomes: Can construct a quadrilateral from 2 diagonals + 3 sides
Can identify which triangle to draw first

micros.title: Constructing with Sides and Angles
micros.description: Construct quadrilaterals from two adjacent sides + three angles, or three sides + two included angles, using protractor-and-ruler sequences.
outcomes: Can carry out both angle-based construction recipes
Can check the given angles are consistent (sum 360°)

micros.title: Special Cases Need Fewer Measurements
micros.description: Exploit known properties: a square from one side, a rhombus from its diagonals — properties substitute for measurements.
outcomes: Can construct squares, rectangles and rhombuses from reduced data
Can say which property replaces which measurement

micros.title: Front, Side and Top Views
micros.description: Draw and match the three standard views of everyday solids and cube stacks — the top view of a cylinder is a CIRCLE.
outcomes: Can draw front/side/top views of a given solid
Can identify a solid from its three views

question.prompt: What is the TOP view of an upright cylinder (like a tin can on a table)?

options.text: An oval that is wider than it is tall
options.diagnosis: Perspective drawings show ellipses, but the true top view looks straight down — a perfect circle.

options.text: A circle with a rectangle around it
options.diagnosis: Mixed two views into one — each view is drawn separately.

question.explanation: Looking straight down at a can you see only its circular lid. The rectangle is the FRONT view (the curved wall flattened). Naming the viewpoint before drawing prevents the swap.

micros.title: Maps, Scale and Location
micros.description: Read and draw simple maps with a scale, contrasting a map's proportional layout with a picture's perspective.
outcomes: Can interpret distances on a scaled map
Can draw a simple scaled map of a familiar space

micros.title: Counting Faces, Edges and Vertices
micros.description: Count F, E, V systematically on prisms and pyramids from nets and sketches — flat faces only — including the hidden ones.
outcomes: Can count F, E, V for prisms and pyramids of any base
Can organise counts from the base polygon (e.g. n-prism: F = n+2)

micros.title: Euler's Relation: F + V − E = 2
micros.description: Verify F + V − E = 2 across polyhedra, use it to find a missing count, and mark its boundary: polyhedra only — no cylinders, cones or spheres.
outcomes: Can apply F + V − E = 2 to find an unknown count
Can state why the relation excludes curved solids

question.prompt: A polyhedron has 8 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges does it have?

options.diagnosis: Used F + V − E = 4 or subtracted the wrong way — the relation is F + V − E = 2.
Solved F − V = E instead — keep all three letters in the formula.

question.explanation: F + V − E = 2 gives 8 + 6 − E = 2, so E = 12 (this is the regular octahedron). Using F + V = E (i.e. = 0 form) yields 14 — one constant wrong flips the answer. Verify on a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2. ✓

micros.title: Area of a Trapezium
micros.description: Derive A = ½(a + b)h by splitting or doubling into a parallelogram: average the parallel sides FIRST, then multiply by the height.
outcomes: Can compute trapezium areas from parallel sides and height
Can recover a missing side or height from the area

question.prompt: A trapezium has parallel sides 10 cm and 6 cm, and height 4 cm. Its area is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied all three numbers 10 × 6 × ... — the two parallel sides are ADDED, never multiplied.

question.explanation: A = ½(a + b)h = ½ × (10 + 6) × 4 = ½ × 64 = 32 cm². Two copies of the trapezium tile a parallelogram of base 16 and height 4 (area 64) — hence the ½. Dropping it gives 64; using only one parallel side (½ × 10 × 4) gives 20.

micros.title: Areas of General Quadrilaterals and Polygons
micros.description: Split any quadrilateral or polygon into triangles/trapeziums using diagonals and perpendicular offsets, then add the pieces.
outcomes: Can compute the area of a quadrilateral as ½ d(h₁ + h₂)
Can decompose a field-book style polygon and total its parts

micros.title: Surface Area of Cubes and Cuboids
micros.description: Unfold cuboids into nets to build TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl) — surface area answers 'how much covering?', a square-unit question.
outcomes: Can compute total and lateral surface area of cuboids
Can choose surface area (not volume) for covering/painting contexts

question.prompt: A box measures 4 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm. How much wrapping paper (minimum) covers it completely?

options.diagnosis: Computed lb + bh + hl but forgot the factor 2 — every face has a matching opposite face.
Summed some faces twice and missed others — list all six faces systematically: two 4×3, two 3×2, two 2×4.

question.explanation: Covering is a SURFACE question: TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl) = 2(12 + 6 + 8) = 52 cm². 24 cm³ is the VOLUME — how much the box holds, in cubic units; the cm³ unit itself signals the wrong quantity for paper.

micros.title: Surface Area of a Cylinder
micros.description: Unroll the curved surface into a rectangle of width 2πr to get CSA = 2πrh and TSA = 2πr(r + h).
outcomes: Can compute CSA and TSA of a cylinder
Can explain the 2πr × h rectangle behind the formula

question.prompt: How much metal sheet is needed for the CURVED surface of a cylindrical tank with radius 7 m and height 10 m? (Use π = 22/7)

options.diagnosis: Used πrh — forgot the 2: the unrolled rectangle's width is the FULL circumference 2πr.
Computed πr², the area of one circular END, not the curved wall.

question.explanation: CSA = 2πrh = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 10 = 440 m². The formula πr²h = 1540 measures VOLUME (m³, not m²) — r² is the giveaway: squared radius belongs to circle area and volume, single r × circumference to the curved wall.

micros.title: Volume of Cubes, Cuboids and Cylinders
micros.description: Build volume as layers of unit cubes — base area × height — for cuboids and cylinders, and keep the units cubic.
outcomes: Can compute volumes of cuboids and cylinders
Can select volume (not surface area) for filling/capacity contexts

micros.title: Capacity Units and How Measures Scale
micros.description: Relate cm³, m³, mL and L, and confront non-linear scaling: doubling every edge quadruples surface area and multiplies volume by EIGHT.
outcomes: Can convert between volume and capacity units
Can state the effect of scaling lengths by k on area (k²) and volume (k³)

question.prompt: Every edge of a cube is doubled. What happens to its volume?

options.diagnosis: That is the SURFACE AREA factor (2²) — volume picks up the doubling three times: 2³.
6 counts the faces of a cube — not a scaling factor.

question.explanation: V = a³, so (2a)³ = 8a³: doubling acts once per dimension — length ×2, area ×4, volume ×8. Check concretely: a 1-cube holds 1 unit cube, a 2-cube holds 8. Lengths scale by k, areas by k², volumes by k³.

micros.title: Grouping Data into Class Intervals
micros.description: Organise raw data into frequency tables with equal class intervals, fixing the lower-inclusive convention for boundary values.
outcomes: Can build a grouped frequency table from raw data
Can place a boundary value in the correct class

micros.title: Histograms for Grouped Data
micros.description: Draw and read histograms — bars on a CONTINUOUS numerical axis, touching because each class hands over to the next, unlike category bar graphs.
outcomes: Can draw a histogram from a grouped frequency table
Can articulate the histogram/bar-graph distinction

question.prompt: Why do the bars of a histogram touch, while the bars of a bar graph have gaps?

options.text: The histogram's x-axis is a continuous number line — each class interval ends exactly where the next begins
They don't have to touch; the gaps are just a styling choice
Because histogram bars are always wider than bar-graph bars
options.diagnosis: Bar width follows the class width — it is a consequence, not the reason.

options.text: Because histograms always show data in increasing order

question.explanation: A bar graph counts separate CATEGORIES (colours, teams) — gaps mark their separateness. A histogram covers a continuous measurement axis: the 10-20 class ends exactly where 20-30 begins, so the bars must share edges. Gapped histogram bars silently drop parts of the axis.

micros.title: Pie Charts: From Shares to Angles
micros.description: Convert each category's FRACTION of the whole into a central angle — fraction × 360° — since the circle's 360° represents 100%.
outcomes: Can compute central angles from fractions or percentages
Can read shares back off a pie chart

question.prompt: A category takes 25% of the total. What central angle shows it on a pie chart?

options.diagnosis: Computed 100 − 25 — the remaining share's percentage, and still not converted to degrees.
Used a third of the circle — 25% is a QUARTER: check 90/360 = 25%.

question.explanation: The whole circle (360°) stands for 100%, so 25% gets 25/100 × 360° = 90°. Per cents and degrees are different scales — a 25° slice is only about 7% of the pie. Sanity check: all computed angles must total 360°.

micros.title: Chance, Randomness and Independent Trials
micros.description: Explore random experiments and equally likely outcomes, and confront the gambler's fallacy: a fair coin has no memory.
outcomes: Can list equally likely outcomes of coin/die/spinner experiments
Can explain why past outcomes don't shift the next trial's chances

question.prompt: A fair coin has landed heads 4 times in a row. What is the probability the next toss is heads?

options.text: More than 1/2 — heads is on a streak

options.diagnosis: That is the chance of FIVE heads in a row computed before any tossing — the first four are already done and cost nothing now.

question.explanation: Each toss is independent: the coin has no memory of a streak, so P(heads) stays 1/2. 'Due for tails' and 'hot streak' are the same fallacy in opposite directions. (1/32 answers a different question — the advance probability of HHHHH.)

micros.title: Probability = Favourable / Total
micros.description: Compute probabilities as favourable outcomes over ALL outcomes — part-to-WHOLE — and locate them on the 0-to-1 scale.
outcomes: Can compute event probabilities for marbles, dice and spinners
Can distinguish probability (part:whole) from odds (part:part)

question.prompt: A bag holds 3 red and 7 blue marbles. One is drawn at random. P(red) = ?

options.diagnosis: Computed P(blue) — the complementary event.
Used 'one of three reds' or 'red is one of the... ' — the outcomes are the 10 marbles, not the colours or the red count.

question.explanation: Total outcomes = 3 + 7 = 10 marbles, favourable = 3, so P(red) = 3/10. 3/7 compares red to blue — that is ODDS (part-to-part); probability always divides by the WHOLE. Check: P(red) + P(blue) = 3/10 + 7/10 = 1.
